There is a particular kind of silence in a library just before it closes. Not emptiness, exactly, but the feeling that hundreds of conversations have politely lowered their voices. Books wait with their spines straight. Chairs hold the warmth of departed readers. Somewhere, a clock practices its small, reliable argument.

Outside, the city continues making its case for urgency. Buses sigh at corners. Someone runs toward a train that will leave without knowing whether they arrived. A restaurant stacks plates behind a bright window. Every light seems to announce a purpose, and every purpose seems to require an immediate answer.

But here, a person can spend twenty minutes learning the name of a bird they may never see. They can discover how an ancient baker measured flour, or why the moon is slowly leaving us. Such knowledge does not necessarily improve tomorrow. Sometimes it simply makes tonight a little larger.

I like the idea that curiosity is a form of hospitality. We make room inside ourselves for something unfamiliar, without demanding that it pay rent. A strange fact arrives carrying muddy shoes and an awkward suitcase. We offer it a chair. Eventually, it tells us something we needed to hear.

The librarian turns off a lamp. It is time to go. We return our borrowed worlds or carry them into the street, where the air smells of rain and engine heat. Nothing has changed dramatically. Yet a bird now has a name, and the night has acquired another possible door.
